Distribution. Cambarus bartonii cavatus ranges from northern Georgia and Tennessee through eastern Kentucky, east central Ohio and western Virginia (Taylor and Schuster 2004). In West Virginia Cambarus bartonii cavatus is prevalent throughout basins associated with the lower reaches of the Kanawha system west of Kanawha Falls and basins draining into the Big Sandy River system. Cambarus bartonii cavatus floodplain populations inhabit the Middle Ohio North, Middle Ohio South, and Lower Ohio basins, and are the dominant secondary burrowing species inhabiting the floodplain (Figure 6). It is replaced in the Middle Ohio North basin in Proctor Creek with Cambarus carinirostris. d.a: Distribution: — Frustulia lacrima is found in lakes in Carajás National Forest in Pará, Brasil. Observations: — Frustulia lacrima specimens often exhibit a valve shape that is a departure from the rhomboid shape common found in typical Frustulia taxa, though there are other linear species inhabiting South America and the southern United States such as F. pseudomagaliesmontana (Camburn & Charles 2000, Siver & Baskette 2004, Metzeltin & Lange-Bertalot 2007: pls. 131 and 132), F. magaliesmontana Cholnoky (1957: 349; Metzeltin & Lange-Bertalot 2007: pl. 137) and F. zizkae Lange-Bertalot (in Metzeltin & Lange- Bertalot 1998: 106). Additional morphological similarities between F. lacrima and F. pseudomagaliesmontana exist, such as the slightly expanded external raphe ends, rectangular internal hymen coverings, lack of striae circumradiating the poles, and appearance of the rib-helictoglossa structure, though the helictoglossa in F. lacrima is slightly more linear than that observed in F. pseudomagaliesmontana (Siver & Hamilton 2011: pl. 147, Siver & Baskette 2004). Frustulia lacrima is also proportionally and absolutely broader than F. pseudomagaliesmontana, which has a length range that overlaps with F. lacrima but recorded breadth ranges of only 6.0 – 6.5 µm (Camburn & Charles 2000) and 4.8 – 6.5 µm (Siver & Baskette 2004). In addition, SEM images of F. pseudomagaliesmontana from Florida, U. S. A. (Siver & Baskette 2004) and North Carolina, U. S. A. (Siver & Hamilton 2011: pl. 147, fig. 2) illustrate the species lacking the expanded areolae seen at the apices of F. lacrima.

Distribution. The type locality of Mazax memnonia comb. nov. is reported in the original description simply as “ Colombia, ” which, as noted by Reiskind (1969), included Panama at that time. Silva-Junior et al. (2024) described M. mokana based on material from the departments of Norte de Santander, Sucre, and Atlántico in Colombia, as well as from Miranda State, Venezuela (Fig. 2). Most likely, the collector of the holotype of M. memnonia comb. nov. was the German botanist Johann Wilhelm Karl Moritz (J. Dunlop, pers. comm.), who lived and worked in Colonia Tovar, Aragua, Venezuela (the type locality of several spiders described by Simon), located nearly 30 kilometers west of Carrizal, a locality representing the only modern Venezuelan record of M. memnonia comb. nov. (Silva-Junior et al. 2024, under M. mokana). Papavero (1973) suggested that the “ Colombian ” localities attributed to Karl Moritz might actually be in Venezuela, stating: “ Probably this is another confusion between Venezuela and Colombia, parts of the former having once belonged to the ancient vicekingdom of Nueva Granada. ” Another possible explanation for the labelling of Moritz’s specimen is that it refers to the extinct Republic of Colombia (Gran Colombia), which existed from 1821 to 1831 and also included Venezuela (S. A. Coboby, pers. comm; J. Dunlop, pers. comm.). According to Papavero (1973), Moritz arrived in Venezuela in June 1835, explored the northern coast, the States of Merida and Trujillo, and the Rivers Apure and Orinoco (Fig. 2), and returned to Germany in 1837. Given the date of the original description of M. memnonia comb. nov. (1841), he must have obtained the holotype during this short period, as he only returned to Venezuela to definitively settle in Colonia Tovar in 1840. While it is not possible to rule out with certainty that the type specimen originated from what is now the modern Colombian territory, it seems reasonable that trips to Colombia (or even acquisition of collections from third parties), if they occurred, took place during his much longer second stay, after the type specimen had been sent to Berlin.
